Soft robotic cardiac sleeves are an emerging class of non-blood-contact mechanical circulatory support devices designed to augment myocardial function while avoiding direct interaction with blood. Their development addresses important limitations of conventional heart failure therapies and offers a promising strategy for physiological cardiac assistance. This Review examines the pathophysiological basis for sleeve-assisted cardiac support, recent advances in soft robotic technologies, and the key engineering and translational challenges that must be overcome for clinical implementation. Finally, we propose a translational framework to guide the future development of clinically viable soft robotic cardiac sleeves.

One emerging non-blood-contact strategy is the soft robotic cardiac sleeve, which provides external mechanical assistance by enveloping the heart9. Unlike conventional VADs that interact directly with blood flow, these systems augment cardiac function through synchronised external actuation of the myocardium9,10. By avoiding direct blood contact, soft robotic sleeves may reduce clinical complications, while their compliant, modular architectures enable adaptation to patient-specific anatomy, pathology, and disease severity. Consequently, soft robotic sleeves have emerged as a promising adjunctive therapy for HF, alongside other advanced strategies such as genetically modified cardiac xenotransplantation, stem-cell-based therapies, and tissue-engineering approaches (Supplementary Table 1). Heart failure (HF) is a leading cause of morbidity and mortality worldwide, with an estimated global prevalence exceeding 64 million individuals, and it places a significant burden on healthcare systems through high rates of hospitalisation and associated costs1,2. Although contemporary pharmacological therapies have improved survival, HF remains associated with a five-year mortality rate exceeding 50%, underscoring its progressive and life-limiting nature. Despite therapeutic advances, a significant proportion of patients progress to endstage disease, characterised by irreversible myocardial damage and severely limited cardiac reserve3. Heart transplantation remains the definitive treatment for end-stage HF; however, its application is fundamentally constrained by the severe shortage of donor organs4. Mechanical circulatory support (MCS) devices represent a principal alternative therapeutic strategy, providing mechanical support to the failing heart. However, only around 10–15% of patients qualify for device implantation owing to high surgical risk and complex prolonged management requirements5,6. While contemporary MCS technologies can be life-saving, they are also associated with substantial complications, including thrombosis, infection, driveline failure, and the requirement for lifelong anticoagulation. Moreover, most contemporary ventricular assist devices (VADs) generate continuous, nonpulsatile blood flow that deviates from physiological haemodynamics, potentially contributing to additional complications7,8. Although recent reviews have extensively addressed actuator technologies16,17, materials development13, and mechanical design principles9, critical gaps remain in the discussion of in vivo performance, patient-specific implementation, and clinically viable translation pathways. In particular, the biological interface between soft robotic cardiac sleeves and the living myocardium (including vascular integration, immune response, and long-term tissue remodelling) remains underexplored within the predominantly engineeringfocused literature, and tissue-engineering strategies capable of promoting durable integration and functional recovery have yet to be systematically incorporated. Despite growing interest in non-bloodcontact cardiac assist technologies, the clinical translation of soft robotic cardiac sleeves is further constrained by interdependent challenges, including durable epicardial integration under chronic mechanical actuation, long-term biocompatibility, implantable and energy-efficient power and control systems, and reproducible surgical workflows compatible with diverse cardiac anatomies. Together, these limitations have restricted long-term animal studies and slowed progression toward clinical evaluation. Accordingly, this review integrates advances in soft robotics with emerging concepts in cardiac biology and regenerative medicine, presenting a comprehensive roadmap encompassing pathophysiological drivers of HF, engineering design considerations, preclinical validation strategies, and translational challenges to enable safe and practical medical application. This review primarily focuses on active soft robotic cardiac sleeve systems that provide dynamic mechanical assistance through external epicardial actuation. Passive cardiac restraint devices and purely electronic cardiac support systems are discussed only where relevant to contextualise the evolution of mechanically assisted cardiac support technologies.

In dilated cardiomyopathy, the ventricle is enlarged and weakened, with pronounced wall thinning (Fig. 1b), a characteristic of systolic failure in HFrEF, where the left ventricle fails to generate sufficient pressure to maintain systemic perfusion25. Externally applied sleeve actuation may enhance myocardial contractility, augment stroke volume, and improve cardiac output, while restoring wall tension and mechanical synchrony. In diastolic dysfunction, most commonly observed in HFpEF, ventricular stiffening impairs relaxation and elevates filling pressures (Fig. 1b)26. Soft robotic sleeves capable of delivering timed, lowpressure recoil during early diastole could facilitate ventricular relaxation, improve filling, and alleviate pulmonary congestion. In some cases, systolic dysfunction encompasses both acute and chronic ventricular failure states, characterised by overstretched, thinwalled ventricles with limited contractile reserve. While cardiac resynchronisation therapy improves electrical synchrony, it does not restore the complex physiological deformation patterns required for efficient ejection. Patient-specific soft robotic sleeves may enable regionally tailored mechanical actuation, reproducing native myocardial twisting and thereby enhancing systolic ejection while preserving diastolic filling26. Conduction system disorders, including heart block, atrial or ventricular fibrillation, and mechanical dyssynchrony, may similarly benefit from robotic sleeves functioning as mechanical synchronisers, contracting in coordination with intrinsic or paced cardiac rhythms (Fig. 1b)27. Patients with advanced coronary artery disease or ischaemic cardiomyopathy frequently develop severe left ventricular dysfunction (ejection fraction <30%) and may undergo coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG). This high-risk patient population may also benefit from non-blood-contact mechanical assistance27. While the majority of soft robotic cardiac sleeve designs reported to date have primarily targeted left ventricular assistance, growing evidence from both clinical and preclinical studies highlights the critical role of right ventricular function, interventricular septal coupling, and pulmonary circulation in determining overall haemodynamic outcome. Isolated LV support (whether pump-based or externally applied) can unmask or exacerbate right ventricular failure, necessitating secondary RV support in a subset of patients. These considerations highlights the importance of biventricular mechanics when developing sleeve-based assist strategies. Recent studies on left and right atrioventricular coupling highlight the importance of ventricular filling dynamics, chamber compliance, pressure-volume relationships, and electromechanical synchrony in maintaining coordinated cardiac performance28. Improved understanding of ventricular and atrioventricular coupling may contribute to the development of more physiologically adaptive cardiac sleeve systems. Next generation of soft robotic sleeves can benefit from architectures that enable differential, spatially resolved actuation across the left and right ventricles, or adaptive modulation of compression to preserve septal motion and pulmonary haemodynamic, particularly in patients with advanced or biventricular HF28. Broader biomechanical and translational considerations associated with direct cardiac compression technologies have also been comprehensively reviewed elsewhere29. These analyses emphasise the importance of ventricular mechanics, haemodynamic coupling, and synchronised epicardial actuation in the development of physiologically responsive soft robotic cardiac assist systems29.

Pathophysiology of heart failure and role of soft robotic sleeves HF is a complex clinical syndrome arising from insufficient cardiac pumping and/or filling capacity to meet systemic metabolic demands, resulting in systemic and pulmonary congestion18. Clinically, HF is categorised into four primary phenotypes based on left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF): HF with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF; LVEF ≤40%), HF with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF; LVEF ≥50%), HF with mildly reduced ejection fraction (HFmrEF; LVEF 41–49%), and HF with improved ejection fraction (HFimpEF)19,20. While HFrEF is predominantly associated with systolic dysfunction, HFpEF arises from diastolic stiffening and impaired ventricular relaxation despite preserved contractility, and now accounts for ~50% of HF cases19. Pathophysiologically, advanced HF is characterised by reduced cardiac output, elevated ventricular filling pressures, impaired baroreflex sensitivity, and chronic activation of the renin-angiotensinaldosterone and sympathetic nervous systems, which promote fibrosis, endothelial dysfunction, and metabolic derangements21. Human cardiac transplantation remains the only curative option for selected patients with end-stage HF; however, its use is severely limited by donor organ scarcity and the requirement for lifelong immunosuppression22. Genetically modified porcine cardiac xenotransplantation has recently emerged as a potential strategy to address donor shortages, with early clinical attempts demonstrating shortterm graft function but limited survival due to immune rejection and risks of zoonotic viral transmission23. Device-based therapies, including VADs and total artificial hearts (TAHs), provide effective circulatory support but are associated with thrombotic, infectious, and drivelinerelated complications24. Over several decades, these technologies have evolved from bulky extracorporeal pumps introduced in the 1960s to compact hard robotic devices, emerging soft robotic sleeves, and fully implantable artificial heart systems (Fig. 3a)31,32. Commercial VAD platforms, including the HeartMate and HeartWare HVAD series, are now established as bridge-totransplant or destination-therapy options; however, their direct interaction with circulating blood continues to constrain long-term outcomes33. Hard robotic assist devices, such as axial- and centrifugal-flow VADs, represent the engineering apex of pump-based circulatory assistance, offering compact form factors, magnetic levitation, and multi-year operational reliability34. Nevertheless, their rigid architectures and high-shear flow environments differ fundamentally from native myocardial mechanics. In parallel, the development of TAHs, including the SynCardia™, CARMAT™, and AbioCor™systems, pursued complete ventricular replacement but has been limited by device size, biocompatibility constraints, and long-term integration challenges35. These limitations prompted renewed interest in non-blood-contact assist strategies capable of acting externally to the cardiac chambers. Early concepts, including pneumatic compression cuffs and experimental epicardial sleeves, laid the foundation for soft robotic approaches that support myocardial motion through gentle epicardial compression rather than intravascular pumping10.

Elements of soft robotic cardiac sleeves As the structural backbone of the sleeve, the soft base layer conforms intimately to the epicardial surface and distributes actuation forces uniformly across the ventricular wall (Fig. 3b)10. To minimise mechanical mismatch, the substrate must approximate myocardial compliance (elastic modulus E ≈20–50 KPa), accommodate 10–15% physiological strain, and retain sufficient tensile strength for continuous cyclic loading38. Actuators are the active contractile elements that convert external energy into mechanical motion, enabling reproduction of myocardial contraction17. Among the various strategies explored, pneumatic sleeves represent the most mature preclinical and translational platform, forming the basis of many contemporary soft robotic cardiac assist systems10.

Once fabricated (most commonly via three-dimensional (3D) printing, soft lithography, or moulding techniques) the sleeve undergoes geometric and conformational validation using 3D-printed or silicone ventricular phantoms. The ex vivo characterisation phase subsequently evaluates sleeve performance in a physiologically relevant environment62. The device is mounted onto a compliant ventricular phantom integrated within a closed-loop hydrodynamic circulation system that replicates cardiac filling and ejection. Key performance metrics (including generated pressure, stroke volume, and volumetric compression ratio) are quantified using pressure transducers, flow sensors, and optical motion-tracking systems. The long-term objective of soft robotic cardiac sleeves is to achieve safe, durable, and physiologically synchronised function in the living heart. Although in vitro and ex vivo testing provide essential insight into mechanical performance and fluid dynamics, in vivo evaluation represents the critical translational step linking engineering function with biological response46,63. Initial in vivo evaluation focuses on histological and biological analyses, examining tissue integration, fibrotic encapsulation, inflammatory cell infiltration, and vascularisation at the sleeve-epicardium interface. Effective integration minimises shear stress and motion-induced irritation, while the development of microvascular networks (vasculogenesis) within the interface layer may enhance nutrient exchange and mitigate chronic inflammation. Conversely, excessive fibrosis, immune activation, or local ischaemia can compromise both mechanical performance and myocardial health. Alongside biological assessment, functional performance is evaluated using a combination of invasive and non-invasive cardiological diagnostics. Echocardiography and ultrasound imaging enable realtime quantification of stroke volume, ejection fraction, and left ventricular end-diastolic volume (LVEDV), reflecting the sleeve’s capacity to restore contractility and diastolic filling10,51. Pressure probes inserted into the ventricular and aortic chambers enable measurement of transaortic pressure gradients and ventricular loading conditions. Thermal safety is assessed using infrared thermography or implanted temperature sensors, ensuring that actuation-induced heating remains within clinically acceptable limits for chronic operation (Fig. 4).

Supplementary structural supports, including sutures or polymeric rings positioned at the ventricular base or pericardial margins, provide additional stability for prolonged operation46. Hybrid anchoring strategies, combining suction and limited suturing, have demonstrated improved fixation and durability in large-animal models without compromising epicardial perfusion47. Embedded sensors enable closed-loop control, synchronising sleeve actuation with the native cardiac cycle while providing continuous performance feedback. Epicardial electrocardiogram (ECG) electrodes detect R-wave timing to trigger systolic compression and are typically fabricated from platinum-iridium or gold-coated silicone integrated within flexible circuits10. Mechanical sensors, including piezoresistive, capacitive, and strain-based devices (often using carbon-black or liquid-metal composites) monitor curvature, wall strain, and actuator displacement. Pressure sensors, commonly microelectromechanical systems (MEMS)-based capacitive diaphragms, record internal chamber pressures to support safety monitoring and adaptive control48. Encapsulation strategies combining medical-grade silicone with parylene-C or polyurethane barrier layers provide effective multilayer moisture protection49. Controllers coordinate actuation sequences and synchronise sleeve contraction with ventricular systole, most commonly using ECG-gated control algorithms50. The driveline provides the interface between internal components and external control hardware. Most current prototypes employ percutaneous drivelines, analogous to those used in VAD systems, to transmit pneumatic pressure and sensor signals51. However, the risk of chronic infection has driven the development of fully implantable, wireless interfaces utilising inductive power transfer and telemetry. Transcutaneous energy transfer (TET) systems have emerged as a promising strategy for eliminating percutaneous drivelines and reducing the associated risks of chronic infection in implantable cardiac assist devices52,53. These systems typically utilise inductive coupling between external and implanted coils to wirelessly transmit electrical power across the skin, enabling fully implantable platforms without permanent transcutaneous connections54. In addition to powering pneumatic or electromechanical actuation systems, TET platforms may also support bidirectional telemetry for physiological monitoring, sensor feedback, and closed-loop device control54. Similar concepts have been explored in VADs and other implantable bioelectronic systems to improve patient mobility and reduce infection-related complications. Despite their significant translational potential, challenges including energy-transfer efficiency, tissue heating, coil misalignment, battery longevity, and long-term system reliability remain important considerations for chronic implantation and clinical translation55,56.

Characterisation of soft robotic sleeves, current methods Development of soft robotic cardiac sleeves typically involves computational design, material optimisation, benchtop validation, and ex vivo and in vivo assessment57. (Fig. 4). The characterisation process is often disease-oriented, beginning with computational modelling and finite element analysis (FEA) to predict stress distribution, actuator strain, and global sleeve deformation under simulated cardiac loading conditions58. Anatomical reconstruction from patient-derived computed tomography (CT) or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) datasets facilitates the generation of personalised ventricular geometries, improving anatomical conformity and minimising shear stress at the epicardial interface (Fig. 4)51,59. Following the computational stage, material characterisation is performed to determine the mechanical properties, fatigue resistance, and durability of candidate elastomers, most commonly medical-grade silicones60 and TPU10,45,61.

Current progress in preclinical soft robotic cardiac sleeves Over the past decade, research in soft robotic cardiac assistance has progressed from benchtop feasibility studies to increasingly sophisticated preclinical platforms capable of reproducing the mechanical and haemodynamic signatures of HF. These studies demonstrate a broader transition from proof-of-concept actuation devices towards biologically informed, physiologically adaptive, and translationally oriented cardiac assist systems. The first major step in this direction was reported by Roche and colleagues at the Wyss Institute and Boston Children’s Hospital, who developed a direct cardiac compression (DCC) device designed to replicate native myocardial contraction using soft robotic actuation61. Multiple materials were evaluated for the internal bladders of pneumatic artificial muscles, including silicone, polyethylene terephthalate (PET), nylon, and TPU, to identify optimal mechanical compliance and durability. This study established the feasibility of conformalepicardial soft robotic sleeves capable of generating physiologically relevant volumetric outputs while closely matching cardiac geometry61. Building on this foundation, the translation of this concept into fully implantable soft robotic sleeves tested in vivo in large-animal models represented a major milestone in the field (Fig. 5a)10. Thin silicone laminate sleeves integrating circumferential and helical TPU pneumatic artificial muscles (PAMs) enabled simultaneous compressive and torsional assistance that more closely replicated native myocardial fibre orientation and ventricular twist mechanics. Despite these advances, current sleeve actuation strategies still do not fully replicate the coordinated myocardial pressure generation and deformation patterns of the native myocardium. In particular, synchronisation between externally applied sleeve actuation and intrinsic ventricular electromechanical activity remains incomplete, remaining a major unresolved engineering challenge for cardiac sleeve systems (Fig. 5c). Chronic epicardial compression may also introduce important physiological risks that remain insufficiently characterised, including impaired coronary perfusion, altered ventricular compliance, arrhythmogenic electromechanical disturbances, or constrictive remodelling over prolonged implantation periods65. In addition to systolic augmentation, several platforms have explored active diastolic assistance through controlled recoil or decompression mechanisms intended to facilitate ventricular filling and reduce diastolic wall stress, although the long-term physiological consequences of such strategies remain incompletely understood.

Additional approaches have explored alternative actuation and power-transfer mechanisms. Han and colleagues proposed a musclepowered biventricular assist device (Bi-VAD) coupling a latissimus dorsi-driven muscle energy converter (MEC) to a DCC sleeve66. This biohybrid strategy illustrated the potential for biologically integrated energy-transfer systems capable of generating physiologically relevant ventricular compression while reducing dependence on entirely externalised power systems66. In parallel, Foroughi and colleagues investigated electrothermal artificial muscles capable of generating pressures approaching physiological left ventricular systolic pressure ranges (Fig. 5d)67. Silver-coated nylon actuators embedded within silicone elastomer matrices generated considerable contractile pressures and ventricular-like volumetric displacement in ex vivo models. A recent proof-of-concept hybrid heart combined pneumatically driven soft robotic actuation with supramolecular polymeric materials to improve biocompatibility while reproducing adaptive cardiac pumping behaviour71. Although primarily developed as a bioartificial heart replacement platform, this work demonstrates the broader translational potential of biologically integrated soft robotic cardiovascular systems and the continued evolution of adaptive, bioinspired cardiac support technologies71. Current preclinical studies suggest that soft robotic cardiac sleeves have progressed from proof-of-concept mechanical systems to biologically informed platforms capable of restoring physiological haemodynamics, interrogating disease-specific pathophysiology, and enabling device testing in large-animal models. At the same time, these investigations consistently reveal unresolved limitations, including challenges in achieving durable epicardial biointegration, maintaining long-term mechanical stability under cyclic loading, ensuring inflammatory and thermal safety, and managing control and system complexity. Notably, most studies remain confined to acute or shortduration experiments, with a lack of chronic large-animal data underscoring the translational gap between short-term feasibility and sustained clinical application (Box 1). These constraints define the context for the emerging technological trends, design principles, and translational frameworks discussed in the following sections. Future translational studies will require chronic large-animal evaluation of long-term device durability, inflammatory response, ventricular reverse remodelling, and survival outcomes under sustained physiological loading conditions.

More recently, Rocchi and Rosalia expanded soft robotic systems beyond therapeutic assistance towards disease-modelling and devicetesting platforms. A hybrid in silico-in vitro framework was introduced using a patient-specific echogenic soft robotic left ventricle reconstructed from cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR) data and integrated into a closed-loop cardiovascular simulator51. This system reproduced haemodynamics of HFpEF, dilated cardiomyopathy, and normal physiology with high fidelity, while enabling direct four-dimensional echocardiographic validation. Notably, the platform demonstrated predictive capacity by evaluating transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) devices, accurately reflecting improvements in effective orificearea, stroke volume, flow velocity, and reduction of paravalvular leak68. Such developments demonstrate how soft robotic cardiovascular technologies may increasingly function not only as assist devices, but also as predictive translational platforms for procedural planning, device optimisation, and mechanistic cardiovascular research. Subsequent work by Rosalia and colleagues advanced translational modelling by developing tunable soft robotic sleeves to reproduce HFpEF haemodynamics in vivo in Yorkshire swine (Fig. 5e)45. Acute modulation of ventricular compliance and aortic loading successfully created characteristic HFpEF haemodynamics and enabled evaluation of interatrial shunting strategies under physiologically relevant conditions45. Despite these advances, experiments were limited to acute timeframes, leaving chronic remodelling, durability, and long-term biointegration unaddressed. Progress in biohybrid cardiovascular systems has expanded opportunities for physiologically relevant disease modelling and preclinical device evaluation. In addition to soft robotic cardiac assist platforms, organosynthetic and biohybrid cardiac models have demonstrated the integration of engineered actuation systems with biologically relevant cardiac architectures to reproduce complex myocardial motion and intracardiac biomechanics under controlled in vitro conditions. These systems incorporate biomimetic ventricular geometries, myocardial fibre alignment, diffusion tensor imagingguided architectures, and biohybrid actuation strategies to emulate native cardiac deformation and haemodynamic behaviour with enhanced physiological relevance28,69,70. Notably, Park et al. developed an organosynthetic dynamic heart model guided by cardiac diffusion tensor imaging that preserved anatomically realistic intracardiac structures while reproducing physiologically representative ventricular motion for procedural simulation and intracardiac device testing69. Similarly, recent robotic right ventricle and biohybrid actuator platforms have demonstrated the ability to simulate right ventricular function under physiological and pathological conditions while integrating biologically derived muscular systems with robotic control architectures28,70. Emerging trends and future directions Integrating tissue interface into soft robotic cardiac sleeves Despite substantial progress in soft robotic cardiac sleeve design, significant gaps remain in long-term in vivo validation, histological assessment, and durable biological integration. Current systems primarily deliver short-term mechanical augmentation, whereas future development increasingly points toward biohybrid strategies capable of supporting sustained functional recovery through biologically mediated mechanisms. Recent first-in-human experience underscores the importance of biologically informed epicardial interfaces in non-blood-contact cardiac assist systems. In a clinical feasibility study, Wildhirt et al. demonstrated a biventricular, pulsatile extravascular MCS platform based on a conformal cardiac sleeve incorporating epicardial electrodes and pneumatic cushions72. Real-time epicardial ECG sensing and adjustable deflation timing relative to aortic valve closure enabled optimisation of ventricular filling while avoiding electromechanical asynchrony72. Adapting sleeve geometry and functional performance to anatomical and physiological variability enables personalised cardiac support that maximises mechanical efficiency while minimising invasiveness and adverse remodelling, establishing a pathway towards bioadaptive, regenerative, and clinically translatable cardiac assist systems. Translational and clinical framework Beyond device design, surgical implantation introduces several translational challenges. Effective clinical adoption requires standardised, reproducible implantation workflows that preserve pericardial integrity, avoid coronary compression, and protect adjacent structures such as the phrenic nerve and atrioventricular groove. While most existing studies employ median sternotomy with partial pericardiotomy, minimally invasive and robot-assisted approaches may become feasible as device profiles and fixation strategies evolve. Achieving uniform epicardial coverage without excessive manipulation or suturing is critical, as epicardial trauma increases the risk of bleeding and postoperative arrhythmias. Clear decision pathways for device explantation or revision are particularly important for biointegrative or adhesive-based designs, where long-term attachment may complicate retrieval. Chronic implantation raises concerns regarding fibrotic encapsulation and persistent inflammatory responses, phenomena observed across long-term cardiac implants and requiring systematic evaluation. One of the most important translational considerations involves the interaction between sleeve-assisted biomechanics and cardiac reverse remodelling during chronic support. Mechanical unloading and externally applied ventricular assistance may progressively alter ventricular geometry, wall stress, chamber compliance, and myocardial strain distribution over time117,118. Consequently, future cardiac sleeves may require adaptive or reconfigurable actuation systems capable of responding to evolving cardiac anatomy and functional recovery during long-term implantation. Appropriate patient selection will also represent a critical determinant of future clinical success119. Soft robotic cardiac sleeves may be particularly suited for patients with advanced systolic heart failure who retain partially recoverable myocardial function and could benefit from mechanical augmentation without direct blood contact. In contrast, patients with severe myocardial fibrosis, restrictive physiology, advanced right ventricular failure, or extensive electrical dyssynchrony may present additional biomechanical and surgical challenges. Conclusion Soft robotic cardiac sleeves represent an emerging class of cardiac assist technologies that provide physiologically relevant, non-bloodcontact ventricular support. By mimicking native myocardial motion while avoiding direct interaction with circulating blood, these systems have the potential to reduce thrombogenic and infectious risks associated with intravascular mechanical assist devices. Despite these advantages, translation into long-term animal studies and routine clinical practice remains constrained by several unresolved challenges. Although acute and short-term preclinical investigations consistently demonstrate haemodynamic benefit, durable epicardial integration under sustained mechanical actuation remains a principal barrier to chronic implantation. Achieving effective force transmission, biological tolerance, coronary safety and device reversibility simultaneously has not yet been realised with existing interface materials and fixation strategies.
